cells.tense: You are here with the pen, and the work has come round to its end.
cells.act: open the door to the next thing on time, not early
cells.ask: Pick what's genuinely finished. Let the next one in as it arrives — right on time, not before — while your hands are still warm from the last.
cells.core:
You get to the end of things and you don't stop moving. A stretch of work closes, and you're already facing what's coming through behind it; the finishing and the starting are one motion for you. That's why the momentum holds — you're not dragging a finished thing along. The people working next to you feel it as clean air coming in behind the work.

There's a small cost worth naming. Because you don't linger, you can miss the moment of sitting with a thing that's done before the next one asks for you. So for the next week, do the closing on purpose: when something is genuinely finished, mark it finished to yourself, once, quietly, then let what's next come in. Don't hold it open longer than it needs. Don't shut it early just to move.
cells.sheetLine: You finish and start in the same motion. That's what keeps it moving.
cells.verb: completing a cycle so it can turn into the next
cells.place: on the moving line between here and where this is going

cells.tense: You will arrive before the work has finished carrying you there.
cells.act: receive the thing that is coming instead of bracing for it
cells.ask: Next time you catch yourself calling something done, stop at the door. Spend a minute receiving what's still arriving — a last piece, a reply, a number — before you close it out.
cells.core:
You're calling arrivals before they land. Out on the line, the goal isn't reached yet, but you've already written the ending — told someone it's finished, relaxed into it, started planning the next one — and the work you were carrying isn't there yet. You can see the shape of done so clearly that you step into it early, and the work keeps being asked to be finished before it is. The momentum you're protecting starts running on air.

Source has another half: what's arriving, arriving. Take something you'd normally declare done this early, and this week hold off the declaring. Receive the last piece as it comes. Not indefinitely; just until it's here. When you stop writing the ending ahead, the ending gets to be real when it lands.

cells.tense: You are standing at a door that already closed behind you, still reaching for the handle.
cells.act: notice what is newly here, right now
cells.ask: Find a goal that's already over and mark it closed, once, privately. Then take this week as it comes, without measuring it against what you were carrying.
cells.core:
Out on the line, you're still walking toward goals that have already arrived — or already ended. Something is finished, and you don't let it be finished; you keep it open, keep looking, keep the search on, because closing it would mean being still long enough to notice you're already there. Meanwhile the momentum that used to carry you is running on an old map.

Here is the small door back. Name one cycle that's genuinely over — finished, ended, done, whatever it was — and close the book on it, once, where you can see it. You don't have to grieve it or celebrate it or explain it. Then take this week plainly, freshly, one day at a time, and give what's actually here a turn. Attending to it does the work.
cells.sheetLine: You're still walking toward a goal that's already over.
cells.verb: completing a cycle so it can turn into the next
cells.place: on the moving line between here and where this is going

cells.tense: You are writing in a room whose last page was already turned, and your hand is still moving.
cells.act: stop holding what no longer serves
cells.ask: Pick a plan or a run of effort whose chapter has closed, and stop holding it. Leave your hands open a while and see what they do.
cells.core:
You don't know which things are over and which are still going. The line keeps moving because you keep providing the motion, and somewhere in all of it, cycles end that you haven't noticed ending — a run of work that's finished, a plan that's already played out — and you're still pushing them forward, like a hand on a door that opened an hour ago. The steering goes on; the recognition of what it's steering has gone quiet.

Faith has a simpler version of the same act: release, on purpose. Take something whose chapter is genuinely closed and stop holding it — deliberately, once, without losing it and without a ceremony. Not forever; a day is enough to start. From there you can see which of the things you're carrying are still yours to carry. Most of them will still be.
